title: Embeddings & Vector Representations
summary: Dense vector representations that capture semantic relationships between words, sentences, and documents in continuous vector spaces.
historicalContext: Before embeddings, NLP relied on sparse bag-of-words representations that lost semantic relationships. Word2Vec (2013) demonstrated that dense vector representations could capture semantic relationships algebraically (King - Man + Woman = Queen), launching the modern embeddings era.

landmarkReferences.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
landmarkReferences.contribution: Introduced Word2Vec, demonstrating that dense vector representations capture semantic relationships.

landmarkReferences.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
landmarkReferences.contribution: Advanced dense vector retrieval for open-domain QA.

commonMisconceptions.wrong: Embeddings store the original data in a compressed format.
commonMisconceptions.correct: Embeddings are dense vector representations that capture semantic relationships. They do not store the original data — they encode patterns and relationships. Retrieval finds similar patterns, not exact copies.

analogies.text: An embedding is like a GPS coordinate for meaning. Just as GPS coordinates place cities in a 2D space where nearby coordinates mean geographically close cities, embeddings place words in a high-dimensional space where nearby vectors mean semantically similar words.
analogies.limitations: GPS coordinates are 2D and interpretable. Embeddings operate in hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and individual dimensions are not human-interpretable.

analogies.text: An embedding is like a library classification system. Books about similar topics get similar call numbers.
analogies.limitations: Library classification is designed by humans with explicit rules. Embeddings are learned from data and may capture relationships that are not obvious to humans.

curiosityFacts: High-dimensional word embeddings connect to geometry. In vector spaces, semantic relations behave like physical directions: subtracting 'Man' from 'King' and adding 'Woman' yields a vector closest to 'Queen'.
Vector searches in RAG databases share mathematical foundations with molecular biology: searching for similar embeddings uses the same cosine similarity formulas used to compare DNA sequences.
storySeeds: The transition from sparse bag-of-words to dense embeddings fundamentally changed how machines understand language meaning.
